party_name: All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK)

founders.name: M.G. Ramachandran
founders.brief: A charismatic film actor and politician, M.G. Ramachandran (MGR) founded the AIADMK after being expelled from the DMK. He served as the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu from 1977 until his death in 1987, known for his populist welfare schemes and mass appeal.

original_ideology: The AIADMK's original ideology, termed 'Annaism' by MGR, was a blend of Dravidian principles, populism, and welfarism, based on the ideals of C.N. Annadurai. It focused on social justice, self-respect, and the promotion of Tamil identity, while adopting a more moderate stance on religion and language compared to the DMK.
current_ideology: The party continues to adhere to Dravidian ideals, populism, and welfarism, emphasizing social welfare programs, the promotion of Tamil culture and language, and state autonomy. It generally maintains a centrist or centre-left position, often being more flexible and less confrontational than the DMK on issues like Hindi imposition and religion.
original_motto: Kodi pidikum thondan mudivedupan (The primary members of the party will take the ultimate decision)
symbol_history: The 'Two Leaves' symbol was adopted at the party's formation. After MGR's death in 1987, the party split into Janaki and Jayalalithaa factions, leading to the symbol being frozen; Janaki's faction received 'Twin Pigeon' and Jayalalithaa's received 'Rooster' for the 1989 elections. The symbol was reunited under Jayalalithaa in February 1989. Following Jayalalithaa's death in 2016, the symbol was again frozen due to a split between O. Panneerselvam (OPS) and V.K. Sasikala factions, with OPS temporarily using 'Electric Pole' and Sasikala using 'Hat'. The Election Commission later allotted the 'Two Leaves' symbol to the unified EPS-OPS camp in November 2017.
headquarters: Puratchi Thalaivar M.G.R. Maaligai, 226, V.P. Raman Salai, Royapettah, Chennai – 600014, Tamil Nadu, India

notable_leaders_through_history.name: M.G. Ramachandran (MGR)
notable_leaders_through_history.legacy: Founded the AIADMK and led it to three consecutive electoral victories as Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu. He was known for his charismatic leadership and extensive welfare programs, particularly for the poor.

notable_leaders_through_history.name: J. Jayalalithaa
notable_leaders_through_history.legacy: Reunited the party after MGR's death and led AIADMK to multiple electoral successes, serving several terms as Chief Minister. She was a powerful leader known for her 'Amma' welfare schemes and strong administrative decisions.

era_timeline: 1972-1977: Foundation and initial growth under MGR, establishing the party as a significant political force and securing its first electoral victory.
1977-1980: MGR's first term as Chief Minister, focusing on welfare policies and consolidating the party's hold on power.
1980-1984: MGR's second term as Chief Minister, marked by continued governance and implementation of populist schemes.
1984-1987: MGR's third term as Chief Minister, characterized by his declining health and eventual demise, leaving a leadership vacuum.
1988-1991: Post-MGR succession crisis, party split into factions, and eventual reunification under J. Jayalalithaa's leadership, leading to a significant electoral win.
1991-1996: Jayalalithaa's first full term as Chief Minister, marked by strong governance and initial allegations of corruption.
1996-2001: AIADMK in opposition, facing numerous legal challenges and corruption cases against its leader, Jayalalithaa.
2001-2006: Jayalalithaa's return to power as Chief Minister (after initial disqualification), implementing various policies and schemes.
2006-2011: AIADMK in opposition, serving as the primary opposition party in the state assembly.
2011-2016: Jayalalithaa's return to power, securing a rare consecutive victory and implementing popular 'Amma' welfare initiatives.
2016-2021: Post-Jayalalithaa era, marked by intense leadership struggles, party splits, and eventual electoral defeat in the 2021 assembly elections.
2021-2026: AIADMK in opposition, undergoing internal leadership consolidation under Edappadi K. Palaniswami, leading up to the 2026 elections.

chapters.title: The Phoenix Rises: MGR's AIADMK Emerges and Conquers
chapters.narrative:
The year 1972 marked a seismic shift in Tamil Nadu politics, a dramatic turning point orchestrated by the charismatic film star M.G. Ramachandran, affectionately known as MGR. On October 10, 1972, MGR, then the Treasurer of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), was unceremoniously expelled from the party. His 'crime'? Demanding that DMK leaders declare their assets, a move that exposed simmering tensions and allegations of corruption within the ruling party. Just a week later, on October 17, 1972, MGR launched his own political vehicle, the Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (ADMK), later renamed All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) in September 1976.

MGR's immense popularity, honed over decades as a cinematic hero who championed the common man, translated almost instantly into political capital. Within two months of its founding, the AIADMK boasted nearly a million supporters, a testament to his magnetic appeal. The party's ideology, termed 'Annaism' by MGR, was a clever blend of Dravidian principles, populism, and welfarism, rooted in the ideals of C.N. Annadurai. It emphasized social justice, self-respect, and Tamil identity, yet adopted a more moderate stance on religion and language compared to the DMK, appealing to a broader spectrum of voters.

The AIADMK's initial electoral forays were immediate successes. In May 1973, the party secured its first victory in the Dindigul parliamentary by-election, followed by another win in the Coimbatore West assembly by-election in 1974. As the political landscape in India grew turbulent with the imposition of the Emergency in 1975, MGR's AIADMK strategically aligned itself with Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's Congress, even supporting the controversial measure. This alliance proved crucial when, in January 1976, the DMK government led by M. Karunanidhi was dismissed by the central government on corruption charges, leading to President's Rule in Tamil Nadu.

The stage was set for the 1977 elections. In the March 1977 Lok Sabha elections, the AIADMK, in alliance with the Indian National Congress and the Communist Party of India, swept Tamil Nadu, winning 34 out of 39 seats, even as the Congress faced a national defeat. Just months later, in the June 1977 Assembly elections, MGR led the AIADMK-CPI(M) front to a historic victory, securing 144 out of 234 seats, with AIADMK alone winning 130. On June 30, 1977, MGR was sworn in as Chief Minister, marking the culmination of a meteoric rise and firmly establishing the AIADMK as a dominant force in Tamil Nadu politics.

chapters.title: The Rise of the Puratchi Thalaivar: MGR's First Stint as Chief Minister
chapters.narrative:
The year 1977 marked a seismic shift in Tamil Nadu politics, as the charismatic film star M.G. Ramachandran, affectionately known as MGR, led his All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) to a resounding victory in the Assembly elections. Having broken away from the DMK in 1972 amidst allegations of corruption against the then-ruling party, MGR had positioned himself as a champion of the poor and a beacon of clean governance. His cinematic persona, often portraying a benevolent protector of the downtrodden, resonated deeply with the masses, culminating in his historic ascension to the Chief Minister's office on June 30, 1977.

His first term was defined by a strong focus on welfare policies, aimed at uplifting the economically weaker sections of society. He expanded existing schemes and introduced new ones, laying the groundwork for what would become the 'MGR model' of welfarism. However, this period was not without its challenges. In a controversial move in July 1979, his government introduced an income ceiling for Backward Classes reservations, sparking widespread protests and discontent.

The political landscape at the national level also played a crucial role. After supporting the Janata Party government at the Centre, the AIADMK faced a setback in the January 1980 Lok Sabha elections, winning only two seats in Tamil Nadu against a formidable DMK-Congress(I) alliance. This defeat emboldened the opposition, and in February 1980, MGR's government was controversily dismissed by the central government, leading to a brief spell of President's Rule. Yet, MGR's popularity proved resilient. Campaigning on a platform of being 'unjustly treated,' he led the AIADMK to another decisive victory in the May 1980 Assembly elections, returning to power and solidifying his image as the 'Puratchi Thalaivar' – the Revolutionary Leader.

chapters.title: The Return of the Matinee Idol: MGR's Second Act and the Rise of Populism
chapters.narrative:
The year 1980 began with a political earthquake in Tamil Nadu. Just months after the AIADMK, led by the charismatic M.G. Ramachandran (MGR), suffered a crushing defeat in the January Lok Sabha elections, winning only 2 out of 39 seats against a resurgent DMK-Congress alliance, MGR's state government was controversially dismissed by the central government. Citing a 'failure of state machinery' amidst farmers' protests, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi dissolved the assembly, forcing fresh elections. Many believed this was the end of MGR's reign. However, the 'Puratchi Thalaivar' (Revolutionary Leader) was far from finished.

Defying political pundits and the formidable DMK-Congress combine, MGR rallied his party. He campaigned on a wave of public sympathy, portraying himself as unjustly targeted by Delhi. The gamble paid off spectacularly. In the May 1980 Assembly elections, the AIADMK, aligning with Left parties and the Janata Party, swept back to power, securing 129 seats on its own and 162 with allies, proving that MGR's connection with the masses remained unbreakable. He was sworn in as Chief Minister for the second time, a remarkable comeback that solidified his image as an invincible leader.

This term saw the full blossoming of MGR's populist vision. His most enduring legacy, the Nutritious Noon Meal Scheme, was launched on July 1, 1982. This ambitious program provided free meals to millions of school children, aiming to combat malnutrition and boost school enrollment. It was a welfare measure that touched the lives of ordinary people and became a cornerstone of Tamil Nadu's social policy. As the 1984 elections approached, a new wave of drama unfolded. MGR's health deteriorated significantly in October 1984, leading to his hospitalization and eventual airlift to the United States for a kidney transplant. Simultaneously, the nation reeled from the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The combined sympathy wave for the ailing MGR and the martyred Indira Gandhi, coupled with Rajiv Gandhi's rising popularity, created an unprecedented electoral advantage. Despite being hospitalized, MGR contested and won his assembly seat, and the AIADMK-Congress alliance achieved a landslide victory in both the Lok Sabha and Assembly elections, marking a period of unparalleled dominance.

chapters.title: The Last Act: MGR's Triumphant Illness and the Unforeseen Void
chapters.narrative:
The year 1984 marked a dramatic turning point in Tamil Nadu politics, as the charismatic leader M.G. Ramachandran, affectionately known as MGR, faced his greatest personal and political challenge. In October, the Chief Minister was diagnosed with severe renal failure due to diabetes, leading to his urgent admission to Apollo Hospitals in Chennai. His condition rapidly deteriorated, and by November 5, he was airlifted to the Downstate Medical Centre in Brooklyn, New York, for advanced treatment, including a kidney transplant. While MGR lay critically ill, suffering a stroke and breathing through a tube, the state plunged into uncertainty.

Yet, even from his hospital bed in a foreign land, MGR's political magic remained potent. The 1984 Assembly and Lok Sabha elections were called amidst a unique confluence of events: MGR's grave illness and the tragic assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The AIADMK, in alliance with the Congress, masterfully leveraged a 'sympathy wave' for both MGR and the late Indira Gandhi, plastering posters of their ailing leader across the state. The emotional appeal resonated deeply with the electorate, resulting in a landslide victory for the AIADMK-Congress front in both elections. MGR himself, despite his absence, contested and won his Andipatti constituency.

He returned to a tumultuous welcome on February 4, 1985, and was sworn in for his third term as Chief Minister just days later. For nearly three more years, MGR continued to govern, albeit with declining health, maintaining his popular welfare schemes like the Nutritious Noon-Meal Scheme. However, the inevitable arrived on December 24, 1987, when MGR passed away at the age of 70 due to cardiac arrest. His death unleashed an unprecedented outpouring of grief, marked by widespread public rioting, looting, and violence across Tamil Nadu, and an estimated one million mourners attending his funeral. The 'Puratchi Thalaivar' (Revolutionary Leader) had left an irreplaceable void, plunging the AIADMK into a fierce succession battle and a profound leadership crisis.

chapters.title: The Phoenix Rises: Jayalalithaa's Ascent from Crisis to Command
chapters.narrative:
The political landscape of Tamil Nadu was plunged into a tumultuous period following the demise of its charismatic leader, M.G. Ramachandran (MGR), on December 24, 1987. His death ignited a fierce succession battle that tore the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) into two warring factions. On one side stood V.N. Janaki Ramachandran, MGR's widow, who briefly assumed the mantle of Chief Minister on January 7, 1988. Her government, however, was short-lived, dismissed by the central government on January 30, 1988, amidst unprecedented chaos and violence during a confidence vote in the assembly.

The other faction rallied behind J. Jayalalithaa, MGR's protégé and propaganda secretary, who proclaimed herself his political heir. The 1989 Assembly elections became a battleground for these two AIADMK factions, each contesting separately. The results were devastating for the party MGR had built: the Janaki faction secured a mere 2 seats, while Jayalalithaa's faction managed 27, paving the way for the DMK to return to power after 13 years.

Humbled by the electoral defeat, Janaki Ramachandran, recognizing that politics was not her forte, gracefully stepped aside, leading to the reunification of the AIADMK under Jayalalithaa's undisputed leadership in February 1989. The party's iconic 'Two Leaves' symbol, previously frozen, was restored. This reunification marked a pivotal turning point. The united AIADMK, in alliance with the Indian National Congress, demonstrated its renewed strength in the 1989 Lok Sabha elections, securing a dominant 38 out of 39 seats in Tamil Nadu.

The ultimate triumph arrived in 1991. Following the tragic assassination of former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi during an election campaign in Tamil Nadu in May 1991, a massive wave of sympathy swept the state. Capitalizing on this, the AIADMK-Congress alliance achieved a historic landslide victory in both the Assembly and Lok Sabha elections. Jayalalithaa, at 43, became the youngest Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, embarking on her first term and firmly establishing her command over the party and the state.

chapters.title: The Rise and Fall: Amma's First Reign and the Shadow of Scrutiny
chapters.narrative: The year 1991 marked a dramatic turning point in Tamil Nadu politics, ushering in the era of J. Jayalalithaa as Chief Minister for the first time. The political landscape was charged with emotion following the tragic assassination of former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi during the election campaign. This created a massive sympathy wave that swept through the state, propelling the AIADMK-Indian National Congress (INC) alliance to a historic landslide victory. Jayalalithaa, a former film star and protégé of M.G. Ramachandran, assumed office on June 24, 1991, becoming the youngest Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu. Her initial term was characterized by a strong, centralized style of governance and the introduction of several populist schemes, earning her the moniker 'Amma' (Mother) from her supporters. She championed social welfare, notably launching the 'Cradle Baby Scheme' to combat female infanticide and undertaking a hunger strike to demand the release of Kaveri river water for farmers. Her government also passed a law protecting 69% reservation for certain communities. However, this period also saw the emergence of serious allegations of corruption, which would cast a long shadow over her administration. The most prominent controversy revolved around the lavish wedding of her foster son, V.N. Sudhakaran, in 1995, an extravagant affair that drew widespread public criticism for its ostentation and alleged misuse of state resources. These accusations, including the disproportionate assets case filed by Subramanian Swamy, began to erode public trust. By the 1996 assembly elections, the tide had turned dramatically. The AIADMK-INC alliance faced a strong anti-incumbency wave, fueled by the corruption charges and public dissatisfaction. The result was a stunning defeat, with the AIADMK securing only four seats, and Jayalalithaa herself losing her seat. The era ended with the AIADMK's citadel crumbling, paving the way for the DMK's return to power.

chapters.title: From the Brink of Defeat: Jayalalithaa's Legal Battles and Resurgent Comeback
chapters.narrative:
The period between 1996 and 2001 was arguably one of the most tumultuous and defining chapters in the history of the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) and its formidable leader, J. Jayalalithaa. Having just concluded a term marred by accusations of corruption and ostentatious displays of wealth, the party faced a crushing defeat in the 1996 Assembly elections, securing a mere four seats out of 234, with Jayalalithaa herself losing her Bargur constituency. This was a political earthquake, leaving the AIADMK in the deepest wilderness it had ever known.

What followed was a relentless barrage of legal challenges. The newly elected DMK government, led by M. Karunanidhi, pursued numerous corruption cases against Jayalalithaa and her associates. On December 7, 1996, in a dramatic turn of events, Jayalalithaa was arrested in connection with the Colour TV scam, marking a significant low point for the former Chief Minister. Cases like the Disproportionate Assets (DA) case, the TANSI land deal, and the Colour TV scam dominated headlines, painting a grim picture for her political future.

Yet, even from opposition, Jayalalithaa displayed her strategic acumen. In the 1998 Lok Sabha elections, she forged a crucial alliance with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which propelled the AIADMK to win 18 out of 39 seats in Tamil Nadu and become a key partner in the central government. This national leverage, however, was short-lived, as she famously withdrew support in April 1999, leading to the collapse of the Vajpayee government. The subsequent 1999 Lok Sabha elections saw her align with the Indian National Congress, though with reduced success.

Throughout these years, Jayalalithaa meticulously crafted a narrative of political victimhood, transforming her legal woes into a symbol of persecution by her rivals. Despite convictions in cases like the TANSI land deal in October 2000, which temporarily disqualified her from contesting elections, the AIADMK-led front swept the 2001 Assembly elections with a landslide victory, securing 196 seats, with AIADMK alone winning 132. This remarkable comeback, however, was immediately challenged, and the Supreme Court nullified her appointment as Chief Minister in September 2001 due to her conviction, forcing her to step down. Nevertheless, the Madras High Court acquitted her in the TANSI and Pleasant Stay Hotel cases in December 2001, paving the way for her eventual return to power.

chapters.title: The Phoenix Rises: Jayalalithaa's Tumultuous Return and the Shifting Sands of Power
chapters.narrative:
The dawn of the new millennium brought a dramatic twist to Tamil Nadu politics, as J. Jayalalithaa, the charismatic leader of the AIADMK, staged a remarkable comeback. In the 2001 Assembly elections, the AIADMK-led front swept to power with a resounding victory, securing 196 out of 234 seats, with AIADMK alone winning 132 seats. However, the path to power was fraught with legal challenges. Jayalalithaa, convicted in the TANSI land deal case, was disqualified from contesting the elections. Despite this, she was sworn in as Chief Minister on May 14, 2001, a move that ignited a constitutional debate. Just four months later, in September 2001, the Supreme Court ruled her appointment invalid, forcing her to step down. In a display of unwavering loyalty, her trusted aide, O. Panneerselvam, took the reins as interim Chief Minister.

The political landscape remained tense until December 2001, when the Madras High Court acquitted Jayalalithaa in the TANSI and Coal import cases, paving the way for her return. The stage was set for a triumphant comeback, and in February 2002, she contested and won the Andipatti by-election by a significant margin, reclaiming her rightful place as Chief Minister in March 2002. Her second full term was marked by a firm, often autocratic, style of governance, including controversial 'midnight arrests' of political opponents, notably DMK leaders. While her government implemented various welfare schemes, the 2004 Lok Sabha elections delivered a stunning blow, with the AIADMK-BJP alliance failing to win a single seat in Tamil Nadu, a stark contrast to the DMK-led alliance's clean sweep. This defeat signaled a shift in public sentiment, culminating in the AIADMK's loss in the 2006 Assembly elections to the DMK-led front, bringing an end to a turbulent yet impactful five years.

chapters.title: The Phoenix in Opposition: Jayalalithaa's Resurgence
chapters.narrative:
The period between 2006 and 2011 marked a challenging yet pivotal chapter for the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK), as the party found itself in the unfamiliar territory of opposition. After a decisive defeat in the 2006 Assembly elections, where the DMK-led front swept to power, J. Jayalalithaa, the charismatic General Secretary, assumed the mantle of Leader of the Opposition, a role she had previously held with fierce determination. The AIADMK, alongside allies like MDMK, VCK, and other smaller parties, secured 69 seats in the assembly, with the AIADMK itself winning 61, but it was not enough to form the government.

This era became a crucible for Jayalalithaa, as she meticulously worked to rebuild the party's strength and expose the perceived failings of the ruling DMK. The political landscape was rife with accusations of corruption, rising prices, and persistent power cuts, which became potent ammunition for the AIADMK. Jayalalithaa, often referred to as "Amma," skillfully capitalized on public discontent, orchestrating large-scale rallies across the state to highlight these issues and rally support against the UPA government at the Centre and the DMK government in the state.

The 2009 Lok Sabha elections offered a glimpse into the shifting political currents. The AIADMK forged a "Third Front" alliance with parties like PMK, MDMK, and the Left, aiming to challenge the dominant DMK-Congress combine. While the alliance managed to secure 12 out of 39 seats in Tamil Nadu, with AIADMK winning 9, it was still a significant improvement from their 2004 Lok Sabha performance where they won no seats. This period of opposition, though difficult, allowed Jayalalithaa to consolidate her leadership and refine her political strategy, setting the stage for a dramatic comeback. The groundwork laid during these five years, characterized by relentless opposition and a focus on public grievances, would culminate in a landslide victory in the subsequent 2011 Assembly elections, ushering in a new era of AIADMK rule.

chapters.title: Amma's Resurgence: Triumph, Turmoil, and a Historic Mandate
chapters.narrative:
The period from 2011 to 2016 marked a dramatic and defining chapter in the political saga of Tamil Nadu, dominated by the formidable presence of J. Jayalalithaa. Having swept back into power in the 2011 Assembly elections, leading an AIADMK-led alliance to a resounding victory, 'Amma' (Mother), as she was affectionately known, began her fourth term as Chief Minister with a renewed mandate. Her administration quickly became synonymous with a slew of populist welfare schemes, branded with the 'Amma' name, such as the highly successful Amma Canteens, providing affordable food to the masses, and initiatives for subsidized water, salt, and lentils. These schemes cemented her image as a compassionate leader dedicated to the common people, earning her widespread adoration across the state.

However, this period was not without its profound challenges. In a stunning turn of events in September 2014, Jayalalithaa was convicted in a long-standing disproportionate assets case, leading to her immediate disqualification as Chief Minister and MLA. The state plunged into uncertainty, and her loyalist, O. Panneerselvam, stepped in as interim Chief Minister, a poignant moment captured by his emotional swearing-in. Yet, the political drama took another twist when, in May 2015, the Karnataka High Court acquitted her of all charges, paving the way for her triumphant return to the Chief Minister's office. This comeback was met with jubilant celebrations by her supporters, reinforcing her larger-than-life persona. The year 2015 also saw Tamil Nadu grappling with devastating floods, particularly in Chennai, which brought both tragedy and criticism regarding the government's response.

Defying political pundits and historical trends, Jayalalithaa led the AIADMK to a rare consecutive victory in the 2016 Assembly elections, a feat not achieved by a ruling party in Tamil Nadu since 1984. This historic win underscored her unparalleled connection with the electorate and solidified her legacy as a political titan, capable of overcoming adversity and securing the trust of the people time and again.

chapters.title: The Storm After Amma: AIADMK's Tumultuous Journey Post-Jayalalithaa
chapters.narrative: The political landscape of Tamil Nadu was irrevocably altered on December 5, 2016, with the passing of its charismatic leader, J. Jayalalithaa, affectionately known as 'Amma'. Her death plunged the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) into an unprecedented crisis, leaving a gaping leadership vacuum that triggered a dramatic and often chaotic power struggle. O. Panneerselvam (OPS), a trusted lieutenant who had previously served as interim Chief Minister, was swiftly sworn in, seemingly a natural successor. However, the calm was short-lived. V.K. Sasikala, Jayalalithaa's long-time confidante, quickly emerged as a formidable contender, first being appointed the party's General Secretary in December 2016, and then making a bid for the Chief Minister's chair in February 2017. This move was met with a dramatic revolt from OPS, who alleged he was coerced into resigning and staged a public protest at Jayalalithaa's memorial. The political drama reached a crescendo when the Supreme Court, in February 2017, convicted Sasikala in a long-standing disproportionate assets case, ending her Chief Ministerial ambitions and sending her to prison. In her stead, Edappadi K. Palaniswami (EPS), a loyalist from her faction, was sworn in as Chief Minister. The party remained deeply fractured, but after months of intense negotiations, the OPS and EPS factions finally merged in August 2017, with EPS continuing as Chief Minister and OPS becoming his Deputy and the party's Coordinator. This uneasy truce saw Sasikala and her nephew T.T.V. Dhinakaran sidelined and eventually expelled from the party. Despite the internal turmoil, the AIADMK government managed to complete its full term. However, the electoral landscape proved challenging. The 2019 Lok Sabha elections delivered a crushing blow, with the AIADMK-led alliance securing only one seat in Tamil Nadu. The 2021 Assembly elections saw the party, still allied with the BJP and PMK, lose power to the DMK-led Secular Progressive Alliance, marking the end of a tumultuous decade in power.

chapters.title: The Phoenix's Trial: AIADMK's Battle for Supremacy and Survival
chapters.narrative:
The period following the 2021 Assembly elections plunged the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) into a profound crisis, testing its very foundations. Having lost power to the DMK-led Secular Progressive Alliance, the party found itself in the unfamiliar territory of opposition, a position it hadn't occupied for a decade. The defeat, where the AIADMK-led front secured only 75 seats against the DMK's 159, immediately ignited a simmering leadership battle between Edappadi K. Palaniswami (EPS) and O. Panneerselvam (OPS), the party's dual leaders.

What began as a subtle power struggle escalated into a dramatic public spectacle, with party functionaries openly demanding a single, strong leader. By July 2022, the AIADMK General Council, dominated by EPS supporters, made a decisive move: it abolished the dual leadership, expelled OPS and his loyalists, and appointed EPS as the interim General Secretary. This bold step was met with fierce legal challenges from OPS, leading to a protracted court battle that captivated the state. While a single judge initially sided with OPS, a division bench of the Madras High Court and ultimately the Supreme Court upheld the General Council's decisions, cementing EPS's position as the undisputed leader by early 2023. The Election Commission of India officially recognized EPS as the General Secretary in April 2023, marking a turning point in the party's internal consolidation.

With internal strife seemingly settled, AIADMK faced the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. In a significant strategic shift, the party broke its alliance with the BJP in September 2023, citing differences and criticisms from the BJP's state leadership. Contesting with a new alliance, the AIADMK faced a crushing defeat, failing to win a single seat as the DMK-led INDIA alliance swept Tamil Nadu. This setback, however, did not deter EPS, who then led the party back into an alliance with the BJP for the 2026 Assembly elections. As the 2026 results began to trickle in, a new challenger emerged in actor Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), further complicating AIADMK's path to power and pushing it to a projected third position, despite EPS securing a massive victory in his own constituency. This era became a crucible for AIADMK, forcing it to redefine its leadership, alliances, and electoral strategies in a rapidly evolving political landscape.
